title: 06. Typing & Models: What is a Dataclass?
summary: Imagine you need to represent a Student in Python. The traditional way:

sections.title: Concept Explanation (Junior Developer Style)
sections.body:
Imagine you need to represent a **Student** in Python. The traditional way:

```python
# OLD WAY — tons of boilerplate code!
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, age, grade, email):
        self.name  = name
        self.age   = age
        self.grade = grade
        self.email = email

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Student(name={self.name!r}, age={self.age!r}, ...)"

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return (self.name == other.name and self.age == other.age and ...)
```

You wrote **20+ lines** just to hold data. Python 3.7+ introduced `@dataclass` which **automatically generates** all that boilerplate for you!

```python
# NEW WAY — clean, fast, auto-generated!
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Student:
    name:  str
    age:   int
    grade: float
    email: str
# Done! __init__, __repr__, __eq__ all auto-generated!
```

> 🧠 Think of `@dataclass` as a **code generator robot** 🤖 — you describe WHAT data you have, and it automatically writes all the boring code needed to make that data work properly.

### What Gets Auto-Generated:

```
@dataclass generates:
├── __init__()   → constructor with all fields as parameters
├── __repr__()   → string representation (nice printing)
└── __eq__()     → equality comparison (== operator)

NOT generated by default:
├── __hash__()   → hashability (need frozen=True or unsafe_hash=True)
├── __lt__()     → less than (need order=True)
└── __gt__()     → greater than (need order=True)
```

sections.title: 5 Examples
sections.body:
```python
# ── Example 1: Basic dataclass — before vs after ──────────────────────
from dataclasses import dataclass

# ❌ BEFORE dataclasses (regular class)
class ProductOld:
    def __init__(self, name, price, quantity):
        self.name     = name
        self.price    = price
        self.quantity = quantity

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"ProductOld(name={self.name!r}, "
                f"price={self.price!r}, "
                f"quantity={self.quantity!r})")

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, ProductOld):
            return NotImplemented
        return (self.name == other.name and
                self.price == other.price and
                self.quantity == other.quantity)

# ✅ AFTER dataclasses (same functionality, 3 lines!)
@dataclass
class Product:
    name:     str
    price:    float
    quantity: int

# Both work identically:
p1_old = ProductOld("Laptop", 999.99, 5)
p1_new = Product("Laptop", 999.99, 5)

p2_old = ProductOld("Laptop", 999.99, 5)
p2_new = Product("Laptop", 999.99, 5)

print(f"Old repr : {p1_old}")      # ProductOld(name='Laptop', ...)
print(f"New repr : {p1_new}")      # Product(name='Laptop', ...)

print(f"Old equal: {p1_old == p2_old}")   # True
print(f"New equal: {p1_new == p2_new}")   # True

print(f"Old lines: ~20 lines of code")
print(f"New lines: 4 lines of code!")
```

```python
# ── Example 2: Auto-generated __init__, __repr__, __eq__ ─────────────
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Employee:
    employee_id: int
    first_name:  str
    last_name:   str
    department:  str
    salary:      float

# __init__ auto-generated — all fields are parameters
emp1 = Employee(
    employee_id=1001,
    first_name="Alice",
    last_name="Johnson",
    department="Engineering",
    salary=95000.0
)

emp2 = Employee(1001, "Alice", "Johnson", "Engineering", 95000.0)

# __repr__ auto-generated
print(emp1)
# Employee(employee_id=1001, first_name='Alice', last_name='Johnson',
#          department='Engineering', salary=95000.0)

# __eq__ auto-generated — compares ALL fields
print(f"emp1 == emp2: {emp1 == emp2}")  # True (all fields match)

emp3 = Employee(1002, "Bob", "Smith", "Marketing", 80000.0)
print(f"emp1 == emp3: {emp1 == emp3}")  # False

# You can still access fields normally
print(f"Name  : {emp1.first_name} {emp1.last_name}")
print(f"Salary: ${emp1.salary:,.2f}")

# You can still modify fields (mutable by default)
emp1.salary = 100000.0
print(f"New salary: ${emp1.salary:,.2f}")
```

```python
# ── Example 3: Dataclass with default values ──────────────────────────
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime

@dataclass
class BlogPost:
    title:      str
    author:     str
    content:    str
    # Fields with defaults must come AFTER fields without defaults
    published:  bool      = False
    views:      int       = 0
    likes:      int       = 0
    created_at: str       = ""  # Will set in __post_init__

    def __post_init__(self):
        if not self.created_at:
            self.created_at = datetime.now().isoformat()

# Required fields only
post1 = BlogPost(
    title="Python Dataclasses Guide",
    author="Alice",
    content="Dataclasses make Python classes easier..."
)

# With optional fields
post2 = BlogPost(
    title="Advanced Python",
    author="Bob",
    content="Let's learn advanced Python...",
    published=True,
    views=1500,
    likes=42
)

print("Post 1 (defaults):")
print(f"  Title    : {post1.title}")
print(f"  Published: {post1.published}")  # False (default)
print(f"  Views    : {post1.views}")      # 0 (default)
print(f"  Created  : {post1.created_at}") # auto-set

print("\nPost 2 (custom values):")
print(f"  Title    : {post2.title}")
print(f"  Published: {post2.published}")  # True
print(f"  Views    : {post2.views}")      # 1500
```

```python
# ── Example 4: Dataclass vs dict vs namedtuple vs regular class ────────
from dataclasses import dataclass
from collections import namedtuple

# Method 1: Regular dict
point_dict = {"x": 3.0, "y": 4.0}
print(f"Dict   : {point_dict}")
print(f"Access : {point_dict['x']}")         # dict['key'] syntax
# No type info, no dot access, no equality semantics

# Method 2: namedtuple (immutable, no type hints)
PointTuple = namedtuple("PointTuple", ["x", "y"])
point_nt = PointTuple(3.0, 4.0)
print(f"\nNamedtuple: {point_nt}")
print(f"Access    : {point_nt.x}")           # dot access ✓
# But: immutable, no defaults, no methods easily, no type hints

# Method 3: @dataclass (BEST for most cases)
@dataclass
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float

    def distance_from_origin(self):
        return (self.x**2 + self.y**2) ** 0.5

    def distance_to(self, other: "Point") -> float:
        return ((self.x - other.x)**2 + (self.y - other.y)**2) ** 0.5

point_dc = Point(3.0, 4.0)
print(f"\nDataclass : {point_dc}")
print(f"Access    : {point_dc.x}")           # dot access ✓
print(f"Method    : {point_dc.distance_from_origin()}")  # 5.0
print(f"Equality  : {Point(3.0,4.0) == Point(3.0,4.0)}") # True ✓
print(f"Mutable   : {True}")                 # can modify

p2 = Point(6.0, 8.0)
print(f"Distance  : {point_dc.distance_to(p2)}")  # 5.0
```

```python
# ── Example 5: Real world — API response model using dataclass ─────────
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Optional
from datetime import datetime

@dataclass
class Address:
    street:  str
    city:    str
    country: str
    zipcode: str

@dataclass
class OrderItem:
    product_id:   str
    product_name: str
    quantity:     int
    unit_price:   float

    @property
    def total_price(self) -> float:
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price

@dataclass
class Order:
    order_id:    str
    customer_id: str
    status:      str
    items:       List[OrderItem]
    address:     Address
    created_at:  str = ""
    notes:       Optional[str] = None

    def __post_init__(self):
        if not self.created_at:
            self.created_at = datetime.now().isoformat()

    @property
    def total_amount(self) -> float:
        return sum(item.total_price for item in self.items)

    @property
    def item_count(self) -> int:
        return sum(item.quantity for item in self.items)

# Create a real order
order = Order(
    order_id="ORD-2024-001",
    customer_id="CUST-789",
    status="processing",
    items=[
        OrderItem("PROD-001", "Python Masterclass", 2, 49.99),
        OrderItem("PROD-002", "Django Guide",        1, 39.99),
    ],
    address=Address(
        street="123 Tech Street",
        city="San Francisco",
        country="USA",
        zipcode="94105"
    ),
    notes="Gift wrapping requested"
)

print(f"Order ID   : {order.order_id}")
print(f"Customer   : {order.customer_id}")
print(f"Status     : {order.status}")
print(f"Items      : {order.item_count}")
print(f"Total      : ${order.total_amount:.2f}")
print(f"Address    : {order.address.city}, {order.address.country}")
print(f"Notes      : {order.notes}")

# Equality works for nested dataclasses too!
order2 = Order(
    order_id="ORD-2024-001",
    customer_id="CUST-789",
    status="processing",
    items=[
        OrderItem("PROD-001", "Python Masterclass", 2, 49.99),
        OrderItem("PROD-002", "Django Guide",        1, 39.99),
    ],
    address=Address("123 Tech Street","San Francisco","USA","94105"),
    created_at=order.created_at  # same time for equal comparison
)
print(f"\nOrders equal: {order == order2}")  # True!
```

quiz.question: What is a dataclass and what boilerplate code does it automatically generate?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Pydantic handles nested models automatically.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Regular Enum members use identity comparison — two members are equal only if they're the same member.
5-Year Exp Answer: > order=True generates __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__ — making instances sortable and comparable with , =.
5-Year Exp Answer: > A dataclass is a Python decorator (@dataclass) introduced in Python 3.7 (PEP 557) that automatically generates boilerplate special methods for…
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: A dataclass is a Python decorator (@dataclass) introduced in Python 3.7 (PEP 557) that automatically generates boilerplate special methods for classes whose primary purpose is storing data. By default it generates: __init__() (constructor with all fields as parameters), __repr__() (human-readable string representation), and __eq__() (equality comparison that compares all fields).

quiz.question: What is the difference between a dataclass and a regular Python class?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > extra="forbid" raises ValidationError if the input contains any fields not defined in the model.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Circular references (A → B → A) require forward references: > > > > For true circular (A→B→A, not just self), use from __future__ import annotations…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Regular Enum members use identity comparison — two members are equal only if they're the same member.
5-Year Exp Answer: > A regular Python class requires you to manually write __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and other dunder methods.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: A regular Python class requires you to manually write __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and other dunder methods. A dataclass auto-generates them from field annotations. Key differences: (1) Dataclasses require type annotations for all fields — they're not just code style, they're part of the dataclass specification.

quiz.question: Why must fields with default values come AFTER fields without defaults in a dataclass?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > These are number comparison constraints: gt = greater than (strict, excludes the value itself), ge = greater than or equal (inclusive), lt = less…
5-Year Exp Answer: > model_copy(update={...}) creates a shallow copy of the model with specified fields changed.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Single raise ValueError("message") gives one error.
5-Year Exp Answer: > This is the same constraint as Python function parameters — you can't have a required parameter after an optional one.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: This is the same constraint as Python function parameters — you can't have a required parameter after an optional one.

quiz.question: What is __post_init__() and when do you use it?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Use @model_validator(mode="after") — it has access to all fields as self.field_name: > > > > For mode="before" (raw dict), access other fields via…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Pydantic handles nested models automatically.
5-Year Exp Answer: > slots=True (Python 3.10+) adds __slots__ to the generated class, which replaces the per-instance __dict__ with a fixed array of attribute slots.
5-Year Exp Answer: > __post_init__() is a special method automatically called by the dataclass-generated __init__() AFTER all field assignments are complete.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: __post_init__() is a special method automatically called by the dataclass-generated __init__() AFTER all field assignments are complete. Use it for: (1) Validation — check field values and raise errors: if self.age < 0: raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative"). (2) Computed fields — derive field values from others: self.full_name = f"{self.first_name} {self.last_name}".

quiz.question: Can a dataclass have methods? Can it inherit from other classes?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > __post_init__() is a special method automatically called by the dataclass-generated __init__() AFTER all field assignments are complete.
5-Year Exp Answer: > These are number comparison constraints: gt = greater than (strict, excludes the value itself), ge = greater than or equal (inclusive), lt = less…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Pydantic v2 (2023+) is a complete rewrite in Rust — 5-50x faster than v1.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Yes to both! Dataclasses are still regular Python classes — the decorator just adds auto-generated methods.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Yes to both! Dataclasses are still regular Python classes — the decorator just adds auto-generated methods. You can add: regular methods, class methods, static methods, properties, and any special methods.
